scope_note: Second-pass research: cross-manufacturer structural engineering methodology and permitting requirements for vinyl fence systems, sitting above any single manufacturer's product line. Complements data/industry-standards.json (pass 1: ASTM scope notes, CSI 32 31 23 master spec, generic post-spacing/frost-line/footing rules, racking-vs-stepping methodology). This pass focuses on: (1) how ASCE 7 wind-load math actually converts to post spacing, (2) which jurisdictions require a PE-stamped engineering letter for fence permits, (3) what a Miami-Dade NOA is and how to read one, (4) the best available frost-line reference data, (5) example PE-stamped calculation packages. Two of the three downloaded PDFs in this pass are real, current (2024-2029) Miami-Dade County Notices of Acceptance for actual vinyl (PVC) fence products -- not summaries or fabrications -- pulled directly from miamidade.gov. Numeric values quoted from those documents (wind speed, design pressure, post/rail dimensions, embedment) are the manufacturer's own site-specific PE-sealed figures for that specific tested product and must not be generalized to 'vinyl fence' as a category.

wind_load_methodology.explanation: Fence panels are engineered under ASCE 7 as freestanding walls / signs (Chapter 29, 'Wind Loads: Design Wind Loads on Other Structures -- MWFRS,' specifically Section 29.3 'Solid Freestanding Walls and Solid Signs' in ASCE 7-16, renumbered to Chapter 29 provisions in ASCE 7-22) rather than as building components and cladding in the strict Chapter 30 C&C sense -- multiple sources (nationalfenceauthority.com, fenceinstallationauthority.com) loosely describe fence wind engineering as a 'components and cladding' problem in a colloquial sense (a fence is an appurtenance that receives wind directly, like C&C elements do), but the actual ASCE 7 mechanics used by practicing engineers (confirmed via a real worked example from MECA Enterprises, developers of MecaWind software) are the MWFRS 'Other Structures' freestanding-wall/solid-sign provisions, treating the fence as a vertical cantilever flagpole fixed at its footing.
calculation_sequence: 1. Establish basic wind speed V (mph, 3-second gust) from the ASCE 7 wind speed map for the project's Risk Category and location (ASCE 7 Hazard Tool online).
2. Determine Exposure Category (B, C, or D) by assessing upwind terrain roughness per ASCE 7 Section 26.7 (roughly a 1,500-ft to 2,600-ft upwind radius depending on edition).

3. Calculate velocity pressure at mean fence height h: qh = 0.00256 x Kh x Kzt x Kd x Ke x V^2 (psf), where Kh is the velocity pressure exposure coefficient at height h (Table 26.10-1, function of Exposure Category and height -- for short fences under 15-30 ft, z is often taken at the code minimum height, e.g. 15 ft for Exposure C), Kzt is the topographic factor (1.0 absent a hill/ridge/escarpment), Kd is wind directionality (0.85 typical for freestanding walls per Table 26.6-1), Ke is ground elevation factor (~1.0 at/near sea level).

4. Determine the net force coefficient Cf from ASCE 7 Figure 29.3-1 (solid freestanding walls/signs), which is a function of the aspect ratios B/s (overall wall length / fence height) and s/h (height above ground of the bottom of the wall / height of the wall -- for a fence built to grade, s/h = 1.0). Three load cases (A, B, C) may need to be checked: Case A/B apply for essentially all fences (s/h < 1 covers nearly all real fences); Case C (which subdivides the wall into pressure zones near the free end, with Cf as high as ~4.07 for the 0-to-s segment tapering down to ~0.55 beyond 10s from the end) only governs when B/s >= 2, i.e. long runs relative to height, and is the case most likely to control post design near corners/ends of a long fence run.

5. Compute total design force: F = qh x G x Cf x As, where G is the gust-effect factor (0.85 for rigid structures) and As is the gross solid area of the wall/panel tributary to the post spacing under consideration (fence height x post spacing, minus any void area for non-solid fence styles, adjusted by a porosity/solidity reduction factor: Reduction Factor = 1 - (1 - e)^1.5, where e = solid area / gross area).

6. Distribute the resulting lateral force/moment into the embedded post as a cantilevered flagpole (fixed-base cantilever bending problem): the post must resist the overturning moment created by F acting at its centroid height above the footing, resisted by the passive soil bearing pressure against the buried portion of the post and footing. This is the same 'flagpole design' methodology CLFMI's WLG2445 uses for chain-link line posts (already documented in pass 1), generalized to any fence material.

7. Solve for either (a) required footing diameter/depth for a given post size and spacing, or (b) maximum post spacing for a given post size, footing, and soil bearing capacity -- iterating until the design satisfies both post bending/shear capacity and soil/footing overturning resistance.
wind_load_methodology.worked_example_source: A full worked numeric example (6 ft x 120 ft solid fence, ASCE 7-16, 120 mph, Exposure C, Risk Category II) computing qh = 26.6 psf and Case A/B/C forces up to ~21,162 lbs total (and per-segment Case C coefficients from 4.07 down to 0.55) was downloaded -- this is the clearest publicly available step-by-step demonstration of how the ASCE 7 freestanding-wall method is actually applied to a fence, produced by a structural engineering software vendor (MECA Enterprises / MecaWind) rather than a marketing source.
wind_load_methodology.solidity_effect: Solid fence styles (vinyl privacy, wood privacy, welded/solid panel) present close to 100% of their face to the wind and use the full Cf from Figure 29.3-1; picket, ornamental, chain-link and other open styles intercept proportionally less force via the (1-(1-e)^1.5) porosity reduction, which is why the same wind map location supports much wider post spacing for open styles than for solid privacy panels -- a secondary source's reference table estimated relative wind load at roughly 0.15-0.25x for standard chain-link and 0.70-0.85x for slatted/privacy-screened chain-link versus a solid panel baseline of 1.0x, but these ratios were not independently verified against ASCE 7 text and should be treated as illustrative, not authoritative.
wind_load_methodology.practical_psf_reference: One secondary source's approximate psf table for a 6-ft solid fence (not ASCE-7-derived, offered only as an order-of-magnitude sanity check, NOT a design value): ~4 psf at 40 mph, ~9 psf at 60 mph, ~16 psf at 80 mph, ~25 psf at 100 mph, ~36 psf at 120 mph. Compare to the real Miami-Dade-approved VEKA PVC Privacy Fence NOA (downloaded, see documents), which is engineered/tested to a design pressure of 17.71 psf at 115 mph 3-second gust (75 mph fastest-mile) -- illustrating that a real product-specific PE calculation and a generic psf estimate are not interchangeable; the manufacturer's own tested/sealed figure governs for that specific product.
wind_load_methodology.key_variables_practitioners_adjust_for_w: Post spacing (tighter spacing = lower tributary area per post = lower force per post), post embedment depth (deeper = more passive soil resistance against overturning), footing diameter (wider = more soil bearing area), post wall thickness / internal reinforcement (vinyl posts commonly add an aluminum insert specifically to raise section modulus/bending capacity without changing the vinyl profile), and fence solidity (louvered/gapped panel designs deliberately reduce Cf to allow wider spacing in high-wind markets -- one manufacturer, Barrette Outdoor Living, markets a louvered privacy vinyl fence explicitly 'designed for warm-weather markets that are prone to high winds' for this reason).

pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.requirement: Any fence product used in Miami-Dade must either (a) carry a current Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance (NOA) for that specific product/model/configuration, or (b) be accompanied by site-specific engineering drawings and calculations signed and sealed by a Florida-licensed Professional Engineer or Architect. HVHZ wind-load calculations are specifically called out as required for fences over 6 ft or in higher-exposure conditions. A Zoning Improvement Permit (ZIP) covers non-wind-resistant open fence types (chain-link non-pool-barrier, picket, iron); a full building permit with engineering documentation is required for wind-resistant/solid fence types and any pool-barrier fence.
pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.confidence: confirmed -- official miamidade.gov Fences and Gates permitting page, plus multiple permit-service secondary sources and the real downloaded NOAs themselves.

pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.requirement: Broward is the second HVHZ county (per FBC Section 202, HVHZ = Miami-Dade and Broward Counties only). Wind load calculations per ASCE 7-22 are required at permit application; contractors must submit two sealed plans covering fence appearance and engineering specifications. Aluminum and vinyl fences specifically are called out by multiple installer sources as requiring either engineer-sealed drawings or a manufacturer NOA/Florida Product Approval. Design wind speeds in Broward run roughly 170-180 mph (Risk Category II), among the highest in the continental US.
pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.confidence: confirmed for the HVHZ designation and general FBC framework (official FBC citation); the specific 'two sealed plans' submittal detail comes from a fence-industry secondary source and should be verified against the current Broward municipal checklist before relying on it operationally.

pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.jurisdiction: Rest of Florida (non-HVHZ counties: Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie, and all other counties)
pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.requirement: A Florida Product Approval (FPA, statewide system under FBC Section 1709.5, searchable at floridabuilding.org) is sufficient in lieu of a Miami-Dade NOA -- a product with a valid Miami-Dade NOA automatically satisfies FPA (the HVHZ standard subsumes the statewide baseline), but the reverse is not true: an FPA-only product cannot be installed in the HVHZ without additional HVHZ-specific testing/approval. Some non-HVHZ coastal counties (e.g. Palm Beach) impose their own elevated design-wind-speed thresholds (commonly cited around 170 mph) that the FPA must specifically cover.
pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.confidence: confirmed via multiple independent sources and the official FBC statutory citation (FBC Building Section 1709.5; HVHZ definition FBC Section 202).

pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.requirement: No single national trigger height or wind-speed threshold was found that universally requires a PE-stamped fence letter. Multiple installer/industry sources converge on the same generic pattern: the Authority Having Jurisdiction (local building department) decides case-by-case whether a fence requires engineered drawings, and this is triggered most commonly by (a) fence height exceeding a local threshold (6-8 ft cited most often as the point where jurisdictions start asking), (b) commercial/non-residential occupancy, (c) location in a designated high-wind zone (coastal Gulf/Atlantic states, Great Plains tornado corridor), or (d) the fence being classified as a legal 'structure' under local code (one source cited an international/general threshold around 1.8-2.0 m / 6-6.5 ft as the point at which some jurisdictions reclassify a fence as a structure requiring a permit). No codified nationwide rule equivalent to Florida's HVHZ/NOA system was found outside Florida.
pe_letter_jurisdiction_requirements.confidence: pattern is consistent across many independent secondary sources, but the underlying claim ('no national fence-specific PE trigger exists outside FL HVHZ') is a negative finding -- i.e., absence of evidence rather than a confirmed universal rule. Treat any specific state/county requirement outside Florida as unconfirmed until checked against that AHJ directly.

hvhz_noa_process.explanation: The High-Velocity Hurricane Zone (HVHZ) is a legally defined area under Florida Building Code Section 202 consisting of Miami-Dade County and Broward County only. Within the HVHZ, exterior envelope products (including fences) must carry either a Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance (NOA, issued by Miami-Dade County's RER Product Control Section) or a Florida Product Approval explicitly endorsed for HVHZ use -- either one satisfies code, only one is required, and an NOA automatically qualifies for statewide FPA recognition (the reverse is not automatic). Both approval paths certify the same underlying thing: that a specific, defined product configuration (exact model, dimensions, materials, fasteners, installation method) has been engineered and tested to resist a stated wind pressure, and that a licensed Florida PE has signed and sealed the drawings/calculations backing the approval.
hvhz_noa_process.what_an_noa_document_contains: Based on two real, current vinyl-fence NOAs downloaded directly from miamidade.gov (see documents): (1) a 1-page cover/scope sheet naming the applicant, product description, approval document (drawing number, PE name/license), missile impact rating, labeling requirement, and NOA number/expiration/approval dates, signed by the Miami-Dade Product Control Section Supervisor (a PE); (2) an 'Evidence Submitted' section (labeled E-1, E-2, etc.) listing the full history of prior approvals this NOA revises/renews, including the specific drawings, test reports, calculations ('Fence and Post Analysis'), and FBC-edition compliance letters, each signed and sealed by a named PE; (3) the actual engineering drawing sheets, which for the VEKA PVC Privacy Fence (NOA 24-0729.04) show: general notes stating the product is designed/tested per FBC Section 1616.2.1 for 75 mph fastest-mile / 115 mph 3-second-gust wind speed at a design pressure of 17.71 psf; a wind-load-rating table; a PVC material specifications table citing ASTM D635 (rate of burning), D1929 (self-ignition temperature), D2843 (smoke density), and D638 (tensile strength); full elevation/section drawings for each fence model (Tahoe II, Breckenridge) with dimensioned post (5x5 in PVC with a 72 in long 6063-T6 aluminum post reinforcement insert extending to the bottom of the post), rail, and picket profiles; a footing detail (12 in square hole, 3000 PSI min. concrete, 6 in gravel fill); and an itemized bill of materials per model. The Barrette Outdoor Living NOA (24-0117.05, Extruded PVC Vinyl Fencing, models Columbia/Imperial/Chesterfield/Breezewood/Brookline) follows the identical document architecture.
hvhz_noa_process.how_to_read_the_fastener_and_pressure_da: The 'Maximum Design Pressure' figures (both positive and negative, in psf) and any fastener schedule in an NOA are valid ONLY for the exact product configuration, dimensions, and installation method shown on the referenced drawing sheets -- deviating from the tested configuration (different fastener spacing, different post size, field-substituted hardware) voids the NOA's applicability even if the base product is the same. This mirrors how window/door NOAs work (documented by several secondary sources on reading NOAs for fenestration) and was directly confirmed on the fence NOAs themselves via the boilerplate 'TERMINATION' clause: any revision or change in materials/use/manufacture automatically terminates the NOA.
hvhz_noa_process.database_location: Public, searchable, no login required: https://www.miamidade.gov/building/pc-search_app.asp (Miami-Dade County Product Control Search). 'Fences' is a selectable Category in the search form (confirmed live on the search page), with subcategory/material filters including 'Vinyl - PVC' and 'Plastic'. Search by File Number (format e.g. 24-0729.04) or by Applicant/manufacturer name. A parallel, statewide search for non-HVHZ Florida Product Approvals exists at https://www.floridabuilding.org/pr/pr_app_srch.aspx (Florida Building Code Information System / BCIS). Do not fabricate or assume specific NOA numbers belong to specific products beyond what was directly confirmed in this research: the two NOA numbers and product names cited above (Barrette Outdoor Living 24-0117.05 'Extruded PVC Vinyl Fencing'; VEKA Inc. 24-0729.04 'PVC Privacy Fence Panels') were independently verified by downloading and reading the actual PDF documents, not inferred from search snippets.
hvhz_noa_process.other_confirmed_vinyl_fence_hvhz_applica: The live Miami-Dade Product Control search (Category = Fences, Classification = High Velocity Hurricane Zone) returned, at time of research, active vinyl/PVC fence NOAs from: Barrette Outdoor Living, Inc. (24-0117.05 Extruded PVC Vinyl Fencing, expires March 2029; also 24-0117.06 'SimTek Fence,' a plastic composite product), VEKA Inc. (24-0729.04 PVC Privacy Fence Panels, expires Aug 2029), All Season Fencing, Ltd. (26-0330.01 PVC Fencing System, expires April 2031), and PlyGem Resid Solut / Cornerstone Bldg Brands (26-0520.02 '6x6 Performance Privacy PVC Fence Systems,' expires Sept 2031) -- listed here only as confirmation that vinyl fencing is an active, populated NOA category, not as a claim about their specific technical contents beyond the two documents actually downloaded and read.

frost_line_reference_table.explanation: No single authoritative numeric national frost-depth table analogous to an ASTM standard exists in the public domain -- every credible source (including the ASCE/USACE-adjacent secondary sources found here) ultimately traces back to the same two underlying data sources: the US Army Corps of Engineers Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL)'s Air-Freezing-Index-based frost penetration methodology, and the IRC's illustrative frost-depth commentary map/table (Commentary Figure R301.2-9 in some IRC/local-amendment references), both of which explicitly defer final numeric values to the locally adopted building code / AHJ. The clearest, most defensible engineering-grade methodology found is the Air-Freezing Index (AFI, in degree-days below 32F) developed by CRREL, which underlies both ASCE 32-01 ('Design and Construction of Frost-Protected Shallow Foundations,' the ASCE standard referenced by the IRC for the alternate FPSF design path) and the state/county frost-depth minimums that AHJs actually enforce.
frost_line_reference_table.authoritative_methodology_sources: US Army Corps of Engineers Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL), Hanover NH -- publishes Air-Freezing-Index-based frost depth maps used as the engineering-grade reference for design professionals (erdc.usace.army.mil/Locations/CRREL); ASCE 32-01 'Design and Construction of Frost-Protected Shallow Foundations' (referenced by IRC Section R403.3 for the FPSF alternate design path, with IRC Table R403.3(1) tying insulation R-values to the local Air-Freezing Index and Table R403.3(2)/NOAA climate data for finding local AFI values); NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information also republishes FPSF/AFI reference material derived from 1951-2010 Climate Normals.
frost_line_reference_table.state_level_reference_table: Best available consolidated state-level table (compiled by a concrete-calculator reference site citing 'ASHRAE and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers frost depth maps, supplemented by state building code minimums' -- a secondary compilation, not a primary-source table, but internally consistent with the CRREL/AFI methodology and broadly consistent with 2-3 other independent secondary tables cross-checked in this research):

state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Florida: 0 (no defined frost line; FBC requires no frost-depth footing provision -- footing depth driven by bearing capacity/hurricane uplift instead; a 12 in minimum footing depth applies statewide for bearing, not frost)
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Texas / Arizona / California (southern): 0-30, generally under 12 in most populated areas; local/county amendment governs
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Louisiana / Mississippi: no defined statewide frost depth in Louisiana (12 in footing minimum applies); Mississippi ~12 in, varies by jurisdiction
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Ohio / Indiana / Illinois: 24-50 (Illinois spans 20 in in the south near Cairo to 50+ in near the Wisconsin border -- largest documented within-state swing)
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Colorado / Wyoming / Idaho / Montana (Mo: 24-60 (varies sharply by elevation; Wyoming ranges from ~42 in at Cheyenne to 48-60 in at higher/northern elevations)
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Minnesota / North Dakota / Wisconsin: 42-60+ (Minnesota specifically codified by state administrative rule at 42 in south of St. Cloud, 60 in north of it)
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Massachusetts / Connecticut: 36-48 (both cited as statewide-uniform code minimums rather than county-amended)
state_frost_depth_ranges_inches.Alaska: 32-120+ (extreme range; interior Alaska can exceed 96-100 in in severe winters)

frost_line_reference_table.design_workflow: 1. Look up state/county frost depth range above (or directly from the local AHJ -- the single authoritative source for any real project). 2. Calculate the structural embedment minimum independent of frost: one-third of total above-ground post height (pass-1 rule of thumb, e.g. 24 in for a 6-ft post). 3. Required post/footing depth = the GREATER of (frost depth + a safety margin, commonly 6 in below the established frost line per pass-1 findings) and (the one-third structural minimum). 4. In freeze-free zones (Florida, Hawaii, southern coastal areas), the frost calculation drops out entirely and wind-load / structural / bearing-capacity requirements govern post depth instead -- explicitly confirmed for Miami-Dade, where post depth in the downloaded VEKA NOA is set at a 12 in square hole (a footing plan-dimension, not embedment depth) sized by structural/wind analysis, not frost.
frost_line_reference_table.caveat: Every source consulted, including this one, is a secondary compilation of state/county averages. Frost depth varies meaningfully WITHIN a single county (documented for Illinois: 20 in near Cairo vs 50+ in near the Wisconsin border) and is frequently overridden by local ordinance amendment even where a state 'default' exists (confirmed pattern: 'Who sets it' column in one source's table is 'County/city amendment' for roughly half of all states). Any BOM pipeline consuming this data should treat these ranges as a planning-stage estimate only and flag a requirement to confirm the exact local AHJ frost-depth ordinance before finalizing post/footing depth for a specific project address.

documents.date_or_version: Article dated February 12, 2021 (Chris Rosencutter, MECA Enterprises); this is a generic engineering-methodology example (not vinyl-specific, not tied to a real project/PE stamp) produced by a structural-engineering software vendor to demonstrate their MecaWind tool

documents.title: Miami-Dade County Notice of Acceptance No. 24-0729.04 -- VEKA, Inc., 'PVC Privacy Fence Panels' (Tahoe II and Breckenridge models). REAL, current, PE-sealed document (not a summary): includes full evidence-submitted approval history back to 2014, and complete engineering drawings signed/sealed by Lucas A. Turner, P.E. (FL License #58201, Turner Engineering & Consulting Inc.), reviewed/approved by Miami-Dade Product Control Section Supervisor Helmy A. Makar, P.E. Contains: wind rating (75 mph fastest-mile / 115 mph 3-second gust, design pressure 17.71 psf, per FBC Section 1616.2.1), PVC material spec table (ASTM D635/D1929/D2843/D638), full post/rail/picket dimensioned drawings, aluminum post reinforcement spec (72 in long, 6063-T6 aluminum, full-depth insert), and footing detail (12 in sq. hole, 3000 PSI min. concrete, 6 in gravel fill).

Miami-Dade County Notice of Acceptance No. 24-0117.05 -- Barrette Outdoor Living, Inc., 'Extruded PVC Vinyl Fencing' (Columbia, Imperial, Chesterfield, Breezewood, and Brookline models). REAL, current, PE-sealed document with a full evidence-submitted approval history back to 2006, demonstrating how a single product line's NOA gets revised/renewed across ~18 years and multiple FBC editions (2010 through 2023).

remaining_gaps_and_not_confirmed: No generic, brand-neutral 'vinyl fence wind load calculation package' PDF template exists in the public domain analogous to CLFMI's chain-link WLG2445 -- every real PE calculation package found (the two Miami-Dade NOAs) is product-specific and proprietary to a manufacturer/PE of record, not a fill-in-the-blank generic template. Searches for an explicit 'engineering letter template' for vinyl fence wind load did not surface a usable generic template; PE letter services (e.g. engineerletters.co, permitsolutions.us) exist but produce custom, project-specific letters rather than publishing templates.

The claim that fence wind engineering is formally a 'components and cladding' (Chapter 30) problem under ASCE 7, as suggested by the assignment brief, was NOT confirmed -- the real worked methodology found (MECA/MecaWind) uses the MWFRS 'Other Structures' freestanding-wall provisions (Chapter 29, Section 29.3), not Chapter 30 C&C. Some marketing/SEO secondary sources use 'components and cladding' loosely/incorrectly to describe fences; this should not be treated as a confirmed ASCE 7 classification.

Outside Florida's HVHZ, no other state or county was confirmed to have a codified, named PE-letter-for-fence-permit requirement comparable to Florida's NOA system -- this may reflect a genuine absence of such programs elsewhere, or may simply reflect the limits of this search; it should not be read as 'no other jurisdiction requires engineering review,' only as 'no comparably well-documented, publicly searchable program was found outside Florida.'

The state-level frost-depth table above is a secondary compilation (not a primary CRREL/NOAA dataset pulled directly); exact CRREL Air-Freezing-Index maps/PDFs were located by citation and description but a downloadable primary-source national frost-depth map/table PDF was not found and not downloaded -- only academic/technical reports referencing the methodology (e.g. ERDC/CRREL TR-19-24) were found, and these are frost-heave research reports, not a ready-to-use design table.
